title: Helicopter Parenting, Self-Efficacy, and Attitudes Toward Becoming NEET: A Cultural Comparison Between the United States and China
abstract: NEET (Not in Education, Employment, or Training) status is associated with poorer mental health and reduced long-term well-being. Because university students are not NEET by definition, this study examined NEET-related motivations among 1,686 students in the United States and China. A new NEET Tendencies scale demonstrated a two-factor structure reflecting expectations of receiving versus providing support when returning home after graduation. Across countries, lower self-efficacy and higher helicopter parenting predicted stronger NEET-related tendencies. Depression showed small bivariate associations, whereas anxiety was unrelated. Cultural differences were pronounced: U.S. students scored higher on the NEET-Proneness subscale, while Chinese students scored higher on the NEET-Mutual Aid subscale. These findings highlight distinct psychological and cultural pathways underlying expectations about returning home and suggest that early interventions targeting self-efficacy and autonomy may help reduce future NEET risk.
